## The Challenge: Predicting Unpredictable Grand Tour Stages

Predicting outcomes in professional road cycling (such as the Tour de France) is an inherently complex Machine Learning challenge. Performance is highly non-linear: rider capabilities, team tactics, extreme terrain profiles ($>4,000\,\text{m}$ elevation gain), and weather conditions all interact dynamically. Furthermore, standard historical features suffer from severe **temporal data drift** as riders accumulate seasonal points over time.

As part of a **university group project**, our team set out to build an end-to-end Machine Learning and Master-Inference Pipeline. Our primary objective was to evaluate how different paradigm classes—**Pointwise Classification**, **Generalized Additive Models (EBM)**, and **Listwise Learning-to-Rank (XGBRanker)**—handle non-linear rankings and feature bias in live race conditions.

---

## Architectural Breakdown & Methodology

Instead of treating stage prediction as a simple classification or regression problem, we structured the pipeline to evaluate multiple model paradigms on identical live feature sets.

### 1. Classification vs. Regression Framing
Applying standard regression to ordinal finishing ranks (e.g., predicting rank 120 vs. 130) drains model capacity on non-critical "peloton noise" in the gruppetto. Following the **McRank paradigm**, we framed the task around ordinal classification targets ($\text{Top-5}$, $\text{Top-10}$, $\text{Top-20}$) to compute expected relevance scores. This focuses model capacity strictly on the decisive front-runners.

### 2. Comparative Model Engine
Our pipeline evaluates four distinct model architectures under identical stage metadata:
* **Explainable Boosting Machines (EBM):** Uses additive shape functions and explicit pairwise interaction terms ($GA^2M$) to prevent individual feature dominance.
* **XGBoost Classifier:** Standard Gradient Boosted Decision Trees evaluating pointwise probabilities.
* **TabPFN:** An In-Context Learning Foundation Model for tabular data.
* **XGBRanker:** A dedicated Listwise Learning-to-Rank model optimizing directly for group-based **NDCG**.

### 3. Tackling Temporal Data Drift
A key finding during live inferences (e.g., Tour de France 2026) was the **Pointwise Feature Bias**: accumulative seasonal points (`lag_rider_points_season`) caused traditional classifiers (XGBoost & TabPFN) to falsely overpredict sprinters on high-altitude mountain stages ($>4,000\,\text{m}$ elevation gain).

We mitigated this by contrasting pointwise predictions against **XGBRanker**. By enforcing a group structure (`group=stage_id`) and optimizing for NDCG, the ranker evaluates riders *relative to the specific stage peloton* rather than as isolated data instances—completely neutralizing the seasonal point inflation.

---

## Key Takeaways

This university project provided invaluable insights into real-world Learning-to-Rank (LTR) dynamics and time-series feature stability.

* **Listwise > Pointwise for Relative Competition:** Standard classification models struggle when feature scales drift over multi-year horizons. Group-based LTR models (XGBRanker) implicitly scale variables relative to the competing group, making them drastically more resilient for future live predictions.
* **Explainability via GAMs:** EBM proved surprisingly robust against feature dominance due to its bounded shape functions, offering a great balance between interpretability and predictive stability on mountain stages.
* **Academic Metrics Matter:** Evaluating models via **NDCG@K**, **MAP@10**, and **Top-K Accuracy** reflects the true business and domain objective far better than standard accuracy or log-loss metrics.
